title: Position, velocity, acceleration, and graphs
objective: Connect one-dimensional motion functions and graphs using derivatives and definite integrals, including reversals and initial conditions.
why: A position sensor records where something is, while a controller may need how fast its position changes or how much acceleration to apply. Calculus connects these descriptions. Signed graphs also reveal a common modeling mistake: returning to the starting point does not erase the distance traveled. You will move between equations, graphs, and physical interpretations and use each to check the others.

sections.heading: Specify what a one-dimensional model means
paragraphs: Choose a fixed x axis and its positive direction, a spatial origin, and a time origin. Position x(t) is a signed coordinate in meters. A negative position means the object is on the negative side of the origin; it says nothing by itself about the direction of motion. The model in this lesson follows one point, such as a cart's center, along a straight line.

The interval of validity is part of the model. A smooth polynomial might describe motion before a collision but should not automatically continue through a wall. Unless a question states a barrier or a change of conditions, use the stated motion law throughout its stated time interval. A negative time from an equation can be mathematically valid yet lie outside the modeled experiment.

For two times with $t_2>t_1$, displacement is $\Delta x=x(t_2)-x(t_1)$ and elapsed time is $\Delta t=t_2-t_1$. Displacement carries a sign and can be zero after substantial motion. Distance is the nonnegative length of the path actually followed; one-dimensional distance still counts travel in both directions.

A polynomial written as x(t)=2+3t+4t² means that its coefficients have different units when x is in meters and t in seconds: 2 m, 3 m/s, and 4 m/s². It is shorthand for a dimensionally homogeneous equation, not permission to add a length to a dimensionless number. Every derivative and integral must preserve this accounting.

sections.heading: Average velocity is a secant slope
paragraphs: Average velocity over a nonzero interval is $\bar v=\Delta x/\Delta t$. On a position-time graph, it is the slope of the line connecting the endpoint events. The intermediate path affects distance but cannot change this endpoint displacement. Moving 5 m forward and 5 m back in 4 s gives average velocity zero and average speed 10/4=2.5 m/s.

Average speed is distance divided by elapsed time. It is not generally the absolute value of average velocity. The inequality distance ≥ |displacement| implies average speed ≥ |average velocity| for the same positive interval. Equality holds when the motion never reverses direction within that interval, including a rest interval.

Do not average two velocity readings without considering what they represent. If a cart spends 1 s at 6 m/s and 3 s at -2 m/s, the displacement is 6(1)-2(3)=0 m and average velocity is 0/4=0 m/s. The unweighted mean (6-2)/2=2 m/s incorrectly assigns the two intervals equal duration.

A finite sensor sampling interval produces an average slope. It is an estimate of a local velocity only when the interval is sufficiently short and measurement uncertainty is under control. Making an interval smaller can improve temporal resolution while amplifying the effect of position noise in a difference quotient. An exact smooth function in a classroom problem avoids those measurement limitations by assumption.

sections.heading: Repair the calculus link: a derivative is local
paragraphs: Instantaneous velocity is $v(t)=\lim_{h\to0}[x(t+h)-x(t)]/h=dx/dt$, where the limit is taken within the model's domain. Geometrically this is the tangent slope of position, not the height of the position graph. A cart can be far from the origin with zero velocity, or cross the origin with nonzero velocity.

For a constant coefficient C and a nonnegative integer n, the power rule gives $d(Ct^n)/dt=nCt^{n-1}$ when n is positive; a constant term has derivative zero. Differentiate each term in a sum. Thus if x(t)=x₀+ut+bt²+ct³, then v(t)=u+2bt+3ct². Evaluate at a requested time only after obtaining the derivative.

Acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $a(t)=dv/dt=d^2x/dt^2$. For the same cubic model, a(t)=2b+6ct. Velocity has units m/s; acceleration has units m/s². The acceleration tells how the signed velocity changes per unit time, so it can be nonzero at an instant when the velocity happens to be zero.

As a readiness check, differentiate x(t)=1-4t+2t². You should get v(t)=-4+4t and a(t)=4, with appropriate SI units. At t=1 s the object is momentarily at rest, but its acceleration is still 4 m/s². If this step is unfamiliar, pause for the linked derivative instruction and return when you can explain why the constant position disappears.

sections.heading: Read speeding, slowing, and a reversal correctly
paragraphs: In one dimension speed is |v|. At a time when v is nonzero, $d|v|/dt=\operatorname{sgn}(v)a$. Velocity and acceleration with the same sign make speed grow; opposite signs make speed shrink. For v=-5 m/s and a=-2 m/s², the velocity becomes more negative and speed increases at 2 m/s each second.

A zero of velocity is a candidate for a change of direction. Check signs on either side and check that the time is inside the interval. For v(t)=t² near zero, the velocity touches zero but is nonnegative on both sides, so direction does not reverse. For v(t)=t near zero, the sign changes and the direction reverses.

At a smooth reversal under nonzero acceleration, position has a local maximum or minimum. Velocity passes through zero while acceleration need not do so. The speed function can have a corner there; applying a derivative formula that assumes v≠0 exactly at that corner would be invalid. Discuss the behavior immediately before and after instead.

Stopping at the final endpoint of an observed interval does not establish that a reversal occurred within it. A continuation might reverse, remain at rest, or follow a new force model. Our investigation reports a reversal only when velocity changes sign strictly inside the displayed interval.

sections.heading: Repair the calculus link: integrate with an initial value
paragraphs: Acceleration accumulates a change in velocity: $v(t)=v(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t}a(s)\,ds$. The letter s is a dummy time variable inside the integral; the upper limit t is the requested time. The initial velocity fixes which of many possible velocity functions describes this motion.

Velocity similarly accumulates displacement: $x(t)=x(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t}v(s)\,ds$. Do not confuse the integral, which is a change in position, with the final position itself. An initial position must be supplied or chosen as an explicit coordinate convention. Neither acceleration nor velocity alone determines an absolute position.

For polynomial repair, an antiderivative of $Ct^n$ is $Ct^{n+1}/(n+1)$ for a nonnegative integer n. Evaluate the antiderivative at the upper endpoint and subtract its value at the lower endpoint. For example, integrating a(t)=2t from 0 to t gives a velocity change t², not 2t² and not t² plus an arbitrary unchosen constant.

If a(t)=2t m/s², v(0)=-1 m/s, and x(0)=3 m, then v(t)=-1+t² and x(t)=3-t+t³/3 in SI shorthand. Differentiate the final position twice to recover the acceleration. Evaluate at zero to check both initial conditions. A solution that has the correct second derivative but wrong initial data describes a different physical history.

An acceleration-time graph has signed area in (m/s²)s=m/s, giving velocity change. A velocity-time graph has signed area in (m/s)s=m, giving displacement. Area below the horizontal axis contributes negatively. Adding absolute areas instead answers a different question.

sections.heading: Derive the constant-acceleration equations and their limits
paragraphs: If acceleration a is constant on the entire interval starting at t=0, integration gives $v(t)=v_0+at$. Integrating once more gives $x(t)=x_0+v_0t+at^2/2$. The factor 1/2 comes from the integral of t; dimensional analysis cannot determine that factor.

The velocity graph is a straight line, so its signed trapezoidal area also gives $\Delta x=(v_0+v)t/2$. This endpoint-velocity average is valid for constant acceleration. It does not apply to an arbitrary curved velocity-time graph. In the variable-acceleration example above, use the integral of the quadratic velocity.

Multiply v-v₀=at by v+v₀ and use (v+v₀)t=2Δx to obtain $v^2=v_0^2+2a\Delta x$. This derivation avoids dividing by acceleration, so the identity remains valid at a=0. However, it loses the sign of v. The actual direction must come from the trajectory or additional physical information.

Do not combine constant-acceleration formulas with a time-varying acceleration by inserting its final value as if it had acted throughout. Either integrate the actual acceleration law, break the motion into intervals on which the assumption applies, or use a justified numerical method. We will study numerical integration later and compare it with exact solutions.

sections.heading: Distance needs the absolute velocity, not an absolute final answer
paragraphs: For a modeled interval $[t_1,t_2]$, distance is $d=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}|v(t)|\,dt$. To evaluate it by hand, find every velocity sign change in the interval, split the integral there, and add the absolute values of the signed displacement pieces. A zero that does not change sign need not change the integrand rule.

For v(t)=6-2t over 0 to 5 s, the reversal is at 3 s. The velocity-time graph has a positive triangle of area 6·3/2=9 m and a negative triangle of area -4·2/2=-4 m. Displacement is 9-4=5 m; distance is 9+4=13 m. Taking |5| after cancellation cannot recover the missing 8 m of counted travel.

Distance does not depend on the chosen origin. Adding 100 m to x(t) shifts the position graph but leaves every position difference, velocity, acceleration, and traveled length unchanged. Reversing the axis changes the signs of displacement, velocity, and acceleration but leaves speed and distance unchanged. These are useful independent checks.

If a problem asks only for displacement, solving for every reversal can be unnecessary: integrate signed velocity over the whole interval. If it asks for distance, the reversal analysis is essential. Name the requested quantity before calculating to avoid a correct calculation of the wrong thing.

sections.heading: Interpret piecewise graphs and model boundaries
paragraphs: An idealized velocity graph can have constant segments joined by instantaneous jumps. Integrate the segment areas with their own durations to obtain displacement. At a jump, the ordinary finite acceleration is not defined; zero slope on each flat segment does not mean acceleration was zero through the jump.

A real cart changes velocity over a finite interval, so a sufficiently detailed force or acceleration model resolves the transition. A simplified piecewise graph can still approximate displacement if the omitted transition contributes little area. State that approximation instead of describing an impossible jump as a measured finite acceleration.

Similarly, position must remain continuous for the ordinary classical motion modeled here. A jump in a recorded position may indicate a sensor reset, missing data, or an unsuitable model. Always distinguish what the graph measures from a drawing of the spatial path: a downward-sloping position-time line means motion toward negative x, not motion down a physical hill.

Use three checks together: slopes link position to velocity and velocity to acceleration; areas link acceleration to velocity change and velocity to displacement; initial values anchor the accumulated quantities. A drawing with an unlabeled time scale cannot supply a numerical velocity or area without additional information.

examples.title: Differentiate a cubic and locate the change in speed
examples.prompt: A cart follows x(t)=2-9t+t³ m for t in s on [0,3]. Find velocity and acceleration, describe when speed shrinks or grows, and compare displacement with distance.

steps.reason: Differentiate position once and twice. The coefficient units make v m/s and a m/s².
The other algebraic root is negative and outside the modeled interval. Velocity is negative before this positive root and positive afterward.
Acceleration is positive at those times. Opposite signs mean slowing; matching signs mean speeding. At the reversal acceleration is 6sqrt(3), not zero.
Evaluate the initial, turning, and final positions to separate the two path segments.
The cart returns to its initial coordinate. The two nonnegative segment lengths add even though their signed displacements cancel.

examples.conclusion: The cart slows until sqrt(3) s and then speeds up in the opposite direction. Net displacement is zero; distance is 12sqrt(3) m, about 20.785 m.

examples.title: Integrate changing acceleration and preserve both initial values
examples.prompt: A cart has a(t)=2t-6 m/s² for t in s on [0,3], with v(0)=8 m/s and x(0)=1 m. Find final velocity, position, displacement, and distance.

steps.reason: Add the initial velocity after accumulating acceleration. The factorization identifies candidate sign changes.
Integrate the entire velocity, including the initial-velocity term, and add the initial position.
Evaluate at the requested final time. The final position differs from displacement by x(0).
Only t=2 lies inside [0,3]. Velocity is positive before and negative after it, so add the two path lengths. The root at 4 s is outside this model interval.
Differentiation and initial conditions independently check the integrated result.

examples.conclusion: At 3 s the cart is at 7 m, moving at -1 m/s. It has displaced 6 m while traveling 22/3 m. Substituting the final acceleration into constant-acceleration formulas would give the wrong history.

examples.title: Use a velocity graph to check a reversal
examples.prompt: At t=0 a cart is at x=7 m with v=6 m/s. Its acceleration stays -2 m/s² for 5 s. Find its endpoint quantities and average velocities.

steps.reason: The negative acceleration first reduces positive velocity, then makes negative velocity grow in magnitude.
Split the velocity-time graph at its zero. The positive and negative triangles have different signs.

steps.math: \Delta x=5\,\mathrm m,\quad x(5)=12\,\mathrm m,\quad d=13\,\mathrm m
steps.reason: Add signed areas for displacement, add x(0) for position, and add unsigned areas for distance.
Both averages use the same elapsed time, but their numerators describe different physical quantities.

examples.conclusion: Position, displacement, and distance are 12 m, 5 m, and 13 m respectively. None is interchangeable with the others.

examples.title: Weight graph segments by their durations
examples.prompt: A simplified velocity graph is 6 m/s for the first 1 s and -2 m/s for the next 3 s. What are displacement, distance, and average velocity? What is the limitation at the join?

steps.reason: A constant segment contributes its velocity multiplied by its own duration.
Distance retains travel in both directions. Average velocity uses net displacement.
The unweighted mean gives equal importance to unequal durations. It is not the time average here.

examples.conclusion: The graph gives 0 m displacement and 12 m distance. Its instantaneous velocity jump is an idealization with no finite ordinary acceleration at that instant; a real transition takes time.

examples.title: Recover the sign that a squared equation loses
examples.prompt: A cart starts with v₀=4 m/s and has constant a=-2 m/s² for 3 s. Use the time law to determine velocity, then check the squared-velocity identity.

steps.reason: The signed time law shows that the cart has reversed. Integration gives displacement.
The squared identity agrees with v²=(-2)² but cannot distinguish the two signs.
The positive square root supplies speed. Velocity includes the negative direction selected by the time history.

examples.conclusion: The final velocity is -2 m/s. A positive square root of the squared equation would report the correct speed but the wrong signed velocity.

guided.title: Keep displacement, distance, and direction separate
guided.setup: A cart starts at x=-2 m with v=4 m/s. Its acceleration remains -2 m/s² from t=0 to t=3 s. There is no barrier.
before: Integrating acceleration gives v(t)=4-2t. Solve v=0 to identify the interior turning time.
The positive velocity-time triangle extends from 0 to 2 s; the negative triangle extends from 2 to 3 s.
Use signed areas for displacement and unsigned areas for distance. Add the initial position only when finding the final position.

question.prompt: Find the displacement, distance, and final position at 3 s. Then describe the speed immediately after the reversal.

options.label: Speed shrinks because acceleration is negative
options.feedback: After 2 s both velocity and acceleration are negative. Their matching signs make the magnitude of velocity grow.

options.label: Speed grows because velocity and acceleration are both negative
options.feedback: The cart moves toward negative x with an increasingly negative velocity; speed is its nonnegative magnitude.

options.label: The cart stays at rest after its velocity reaches zero
options.feedback: The acceleration continues after the zero of velocity. A momentary stop is not an interval of rest.

hints: The signed areas are +4 m and -1 m.
Their signed sum is 3 m; the sum of their magnitudes is 5 m.
Add x(0)=-2 m to displacement to obtain x(3)=1 m. After 2 s, v and a have the same negative sign.
explanation: The reversal occurs at t=2 s. The two triangular areas give displacement 4-1=3 m and distance 4+1=5 m.
Final position is -2+3=1 m. After the reversal velocity is negative and becomes more negative under a=-2 m/s², so speed increases.
question.answerSummary: Displacement 3 m; distance 5 m; final position 1 m; speed grows after reversal.

guided.after: Check your result by integrating v(t) for displacement and evaluating x(t)=-2+4t-t² at 0, 2, and 3 s. The two methods describe the same trajectory.

interaction.prompt: Predict displacement, distance, final velocity, and whether direction reverses inside the interval. Reveal the three linked graphs and compare their slopes and areas. Then change one initial condition at a time and explain the effect.

summary: Velocity is the derivative of position; acceleration is the derivative of velocity. Their units track the time derivatives.
Definite integrals give changes. Add the given initial velocity and initial position when reconstructing a trajectory.
Speed is |v|. Away from v=0 it grows when v and a have the same sign and shrinks when their signs oppose.
A zero of velocity is a reversal only if its sign changes; also enforce the modeled time interval.
Signed velocity-time area is displacement. Distance adds the unsigned travel pieces, splitting at reversals.
Constant-acceleration equations require constant acceleration throughout the relevant interval. The squared-velocity identity loses direction.
Use slopes, areas, dimensions, initial conditions, and coordinate changes as complementary checks.
retrieval: Without looking back, analyze x(t)=3-4t+t² m on 0≤t≤5 s. Find velocity, acceleration, turning time, displacement, distance, and the final direction. Explain what changes if the spatial origin is shifted by 100 m. Check by both graph areas and position differences.
